lessons.title: Plant Morphology: Roots, Stems, Leaves, and Head
lessons.body:
Sunflower is a deep-rooted crop. The taproot can reach 1.5 to 2 meters in good soil, with lateral roots spreading up to 1 meter. This deep root system helps the plant survive dry spells. In poor, shallow soils, roots may only go 50 cm deep, making the plant vulnerable to drought. To encourage deep rooting, plough to 30 cm before planting. Avoid compacted layers.

The stem is thick and sturdy, often 2 to 3 meters tall in local varieties, but hybrid varieties may be 1.5 to 2 meters. The stem carries leaves and supports the head. It is green when young, turning brown at maturity. A single plant can have 20 to 30 leaves. Leaves are large, heart-shaped, and arranged alternately on the stem. They capture sunlight for photosynthesis. In dense plantings, lower leaves may die from shading.

The head is actually a composite flower, made of hundreds of tiny flowers called florets. The outer yellow petals are ray florets; they attract pollinators. The inner disc florets are where seeds form. Each disc floret can produce one seed. A single head may contain 1,000 to 2,000 seeds. The head follows the sun when young (heliotropism), but once mature, it faces east permanently.

Understanding morphology helps you manage the crop. For example, deep roots mean you can apply fertiliser before planting. Tall stems may need wider spacing to avoid lodging. Large heads need adequate water during flowering. When you scout your field, check root depth by digging a small pit, inspect leaves for pests, and monitor head development. This basic knowledge guides all your decisions.

lessons.title: Germination and Seedling Development
lessons.body:
Sunflower seeds germinate when soil temperature is at least 8Â°C, but optimum is 20-25Â°C. In most of Africa, you can plant with the first rains. Germination takes 5-10 days. The seed absorbs water, the root emerges first, then the shoot. A good seed lot should have over 85% germination. Test by placing 100 seeds in moist cloth for 7 days; count how many sprout.

Seedling emergence: The hypocotyl (stem below seed leaves) pushes up, pulling the seed coat above ground. The seed leaves (cotyledons) open and turn green. These are not true leaves; they provide food for the young plant. The first true leaves appear about 10-14 days after planting. At this stage, the plant is very vulnerable to pests like cutworms, birds, and rodents. Keep the field clean and monitor daily.

Spacing matters. For local tall varieties, plant 75 cm between rows and 30 cm within rows. For dwarf hybrids, 60 cm x 25 cm. This gives 40,000 to 60,000 plants per hectare. Thin to one plant per station when seedlings are 10-15 cm tall. Weeding should be done early; weeds compete for water and nutrients. A hoe or hand pulling works well.

Water: Seedlings need consistent moisture but not waterlogging. If dry spells occur, water lightly every 2-3 days. Avoid overhead irrigation in the evening to prevent fungal diseases. Fertiliser: Apply a starter fertiliser like DAP (18-46-0) at planting, 100 kg per hectare. Place it 5 cm to the side of the seed, not directly on it. This gives seedlings a strong start. By 3-4 weeks, the plant has 4-6 true leaves and enters rapid growth.

lessons.title: Vegetative Growth and Leaf Area Development
lessons.body:
From 4 weeks to about 8 weeks after planting, sunflower grows rapidly. This is the vegetative phase. The stem elongates, and new leaves appear every 2-3 days. Leaf area increases, capturing more sunlight. By the end of this phase, the plant may be 1-2 meters tall and have 20-25 leaves. This is when the plant builds the factory that will produce seeds.

Nutrient demand is high. Sunflower needs nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), and potassium (K). A soil test is best. If not available, apply 100 kg/ha of NPK 20-10-10 at 4 weeks, then top-dress with 50 kg/ha urea at 6 weeks. Place fertiliser 10 cm from the plant and cover with soil. Lack of nitrogen causes pale, small leaves; phosphorus deficiency gives purplish stems; potassium shortage causes leaf edge burn.

Water: The crop needs 500-600 mm of water over the season. During vegetative growth, it uses 3-5 mm per day. In dry areas, irrigate every 7-10 days. Avoid water stress; it reduces leaf area and final yield. Mulching with crop residues helps conserve moisture and suppress weeds.

Pest and disease scouting: Check weekly for aphids, whiteflies, and leaf-eating caterpillars. Aphids cluster on young leaves; spray with soapy water (10 g soap per litre) or neem extract. Diseases like downy mildew show yellow patches on upper leaf surface and white fungus underneath. Remove infected plants. Keep field free of weeds; they host pests. By 8 weeks, the growing point changes from leaf production to flower bud initiation. This is the shift to reproductive stage.

lessons.title: Reproductive Phase: Bud Formation to Flowering
lessons.body:
At about 8 weeks, a small bud appears at the top of the stem. This is the reproductive phase. The bud grows rapidly, and the head forms. From bud initiation to flowering takes 2-3 weeks. During this time, the plant needs plenty of water and nutrients. Water stress now can reduce seed number and size. Keep soil moist but not soggy.

Flowering begins when the outer ray petals open. The disc florets open from the outside inward over 5-10 days. Each floret is fertile for a short time. Pollination is mainly by bees, but wind helps too. Encourage bees by avoiding pesticides during flowering. If few bees, you can hand-pollinate by gently rubbing heads together in the morning. Flowering lasts 2-3 weeks. A single head may produce pollen for 1-2 weeks.

Nutrient needs: At flowering, the plant takes up most of its nitrogen and potassium. If leaves are pale, apply 50 kg/ha urea at early flowering. But avoid excess nitrogen, which delays maturity and reduces oil content. Boron deficiency can cause empty seeds; apply 10 kg/ha borax if soil is deficient. Check with local extension officer.

Pests: During flowering, watch for head-eating caterpillars (Helicoverpa). They bore into the head and eat seeds. Scout early morning; handpick and destroy. For severe infestations, spray Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) at 2 g/litre. Diseases like head rot (Sclerotinia) appear as white mould on the back of the head. Remove infected heads. Also, birds can be a problem; use scarecrows or reflective tape. After flowering, petals drop, and seeds begin to fill.

lessons.title: Seed Development and Maturity Stages
lessons.body:
After flowering, seeds develop inside the head. This takes 30-45 days, depending on variety and weather. The stages are: seed filling (milk stage), dough stage, and physiological maturity. At milk stage, seeds are soft and white; you can squeeze them and a milky liquid comes out. At dough stage, seeds are firmer and dough-like. At physiological maturity, seeds are hard and black or striped, and the back of the head turns yellow-brown.

During seed filling, the plant needs water. Drought stress now reduces seed size and oil content. Irrigate if rainfall is less than 20 mm per week. But too much water near maturity can cause lodging and head rot. Stop irrigation when the back of the head turns brown. Birds are a major threat; they eat seeds as they mature. Use bird scarers, netting, or plant early to avoid peak bird season.

Harvesting: Harvest when the back of the head is brown and seeds are hard (about 20% moisture). If you leave too long, seeds shatter and are lost. Cut heads with a sickle or knife, leaving 10-15 cm of stem. Dry heads in the sun on a tarpaulin for 3-5 days. Then thresh by beating with a stick or rubbing by hand. Winnow to remove chaff. Store seeds in dry, cool place in sacks. For oil extraction, seeds should be below 10% moisture.

Yield: A good crop can yield 1.5 to 2.5 tonnes per hectare for local varieties, up to 3 tonnes for hybrids. Record your yields to improve next season. Also, save some seeds from the best plants for planting, but be aware that hybrids may not breed true.

lessons.title: Growth Stage Identification and Its Management Implications
lessons.body:
Knowing the growth stage helps you apply the right management at the right time. Sunflower growth can be divided into vegetative (V) and reproductive (R) stages. Vegetative stages: VE (emergence), V1 (first true leaf), V2 (second leaf), up to Vn (n leaves). Reproductive stages: R1 (bud visible), R2 (bud 2 cm above nearest leaf), R3 (bud 10 cm above), R4 (inflorescence opening), R5 (flowering), R6 (flowering complete), R7 (back of head yellow), R8 (back of head brown), R9 (physiological maturity).

Management by stage: At V stages, focus on weeding, thinning, and fertiliser. At V4-V6, apply nitrogen. At R1, ensure adequate water; this is critical for seed number. At R5, protect pollinators and scout for head pests. At R7-R8, reduce irrigation and prepare for harvest. At R9, harvest promptly to avoid shattering.

Tools for stage identification: A notebook, a measuring tape, and a hand lens. Walk your field weekly. Randomly select 10 plants, record their stage. Calculate the average. This tells you the field's progress. For example, if 50% of plants are at R5, you know flowering is peaking. Then you can time pesticide application (if needed) to avoid harming bees.

Common mistakes: Applying nitrogen late (after R5) causes excessive leaf growth and delays maturity. Irrigating after R8 causes head rot. Harvesting too early gives low oil and shrivelled seeds. Harvesting too late causes shattering. By matching actions to stages, you maximise yield. Share this knowledge with neighbours; collective timing helps control pests and diseases.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sunflower Growth Stage Identification and Its Management Implications

For African sunflower growers â from Tanzania's central plateau to Zambia's commercial farms, from South Africa's Free State to Ethiopia's Rift Valley â the difference between a 1.2 t/ha crop and a 2.5 t/ha crop is rarely about seed genetics alone. It is about timing. Sunflower is a crop that punishes late decisions: a missed nitrogen top-dress, a delayed rust spray, or a skipped pollinator visit each shaves yield that cannot be recovered. This practical reference gives you a field-ready framework for identifying growth stages and translating each stage into a management action with a clear commercial payoff.

The industry standard for describing sunflower development is the Schneiter and Miller (1981) growth staging system, adapted from the earlier work of Schneiter et al. (1981) and still cited in FAO and national extension materials. It divides the crop into vegetative stages (V) and reproductive stages (R), with the critical distinction that VE to Vn counts true leaves, while R1 to R9 tracks the reproductive timeline from bud to physiological maturity. Understanding this system is not academic â it is the language buyers, insurers, and agronomists use when they assess your crop.

Why Stage Identification Drives Profit

Every management input in sunflower has a window. Nitrogen applied after R1 is largely wasted â the plant has already committed its yield potential. Insecticide applied after R6 for seed weevil is too late to protect the seed. Fungicide for rust must go on before symptoms spread across the upper leaves. In commercial terms, stage identification is a risk-management tool: it tells you where your money still has leverage and where it no longer does.

Across African production systems, the most common yield-limiting mistakes are:

  • Late top-dressing â nitrogen applied after V8âR1 is poorly recovered.
  • Missed R1 fungicide â rust and alternaria infections at bud stage can cut yield by 20â40%.
  • Pollinator neglect â bee visits during R5.1âR6 can lift seed set by 10â25%.
  • Premature harvest â harvesting before R9 gives high moisture, low oil, and shrivelled seed.

Data Table 1: Growth Stage Identification and Management Actions

Stage Visual Indicator Approx. Days After Emergence (tropical) Management Action Commercial Impact
VE Cotyledons above soil 0â7 Check plant population; gap-fill if below 75% of target Population sets ceiling yield
V4âV6 4â6 true leaves, rapid leaf expansion 15â25 First weeding; apply basal P and K if not done at planting; top-dress N Weeds at this stage can cut yield 30â50%
V8âV12 8â12 true leaves, stem elongation 25â40 Final N top-dress; scout for cutworm and grasshopper Last window for N recovery
R1 Reproductive bud visible above youngest leaf 35â45 Apply fungicide if rust/alternaria history; scout for head moth Protects yield potential
R4 Inflorescence opening, ray florets visible 45â55 Ensure pollinators present; avoid insecticide sprays Bee visits raise seed set 10â25%
R5.1âR6 Flowering begins to complete 55â85 Monitor moisture; irrigate if available; no insecticide Critical yield window
R7âR8 Back of head turning yellow to brown 85â100 Scout for birds; prepare harvest equipment Bird damage can reach 20%
R9 Bracts brown, seed moisture ~10â12% 100â120 Harvest promptly; avoid shattering losses Oil and grade quality peak

Source: Adapted from Schneiter & Miller (1981); FAO (2021) Sunflower Cultivation Guidelines; and national extension materials from Kenya (KALRO) and Tanzania (TARI).

Data Table 2: Critical Input Windows and Economic Returns

Input Optimal Stage Late Application Consequence Indicative Yield Impact Approx. Cost (USD/ha)
Nitrogen top-dress V6âV8 Poor recovery, leaf burn, wasted input +15â25% vs. no top-dress 40â80
Fungicide (rust/alternaria) R1âR3 Disease established; reduced efficacy +20â40% in high-pressure seasons 25â50
Insecticide (head moth) R3âR4 Larvae inside head; no control +10â20% 15â30
Pollinator management R5.1âR6 Missed pollination; poor seed set +10â25% 0â20 (hive rental)
Harvest timing R9 High moisture, low oil, shrivelled seed â10â30% grade loss â

Source: Compiled from FAO (2021); CIMMYT/Syngenta agronomy bulletins; and African sunflower value chain reports (2020â2023). Costs are indicative and vary by country and season.

â  SAFETY WARNING:

Sunflower heads at R5âR6 attract bees and other pollinators. Do not apply insecticide during flowering (R5.1âR6). Insecticides are toxic to bees and will reduce pollination, cutting seed set and yield. If pest pressure demands action, use bee-safe products and apply in the late evening when pollinators are inactive. Always follow label directions and wear personal protective equipment (PPE). In areas with known bee populations, notify neighbouring beekeepers before any spray operation.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Scout weekly from VE. Record stage, plant population, and pest/disease presence in a field notebook or mobile app.
  2. Top-dress nitrogen by V8. After V8, nitrogen recovery drops sharply â do not delay.
  3. Apply fungicide at R1 if disease history exists. Rust and alternaria are yield thieves; early protection pays.
  4. Protect pollinators at R5.1âR6. No insecticide during flowering. Consider renting hives where available.
  5. Monitor moisture at R4âR6. Drought stress during flowering and seed fill directly reduces oil content and seed weight.
  6. Scout for birds at R7âR8. Bird damage can reach 20%; consider bird scarers or netting in high-value fields.
  7. Harvest at R9. Check seed moisture (target 10â12%); do not wait for shattering losses.
  8. Record everything. Stage-by-stage records build the data you need for next season's decisions and for buyer/insurer verification.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Sunflower Cultivation Guidelines (2021) â comprehensive production and stage management reference.
  • KALRO (Kenya Agricultural and Livestock Research Organization) â sunflower agronomy and variety guides for East Africa.
  • TARI (Tanzania Agricultural Research Institute) â national sunflower research and extension bulletins.
  • ARC (Agricultural Research Council, South Africa) â sunflower production guidelines and pest management.
  • Schneiter & Miller (1981) â Original growth stage description (Crop Science) â the foundational scientific paper.

This module is part of the Rise Africa Skills â Sunflower Farming course. Always verify local recommendations with your national extension service before applying inputs.

quiz.q: How deep can sunflower roots grow in good soil?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower has a deep taproot that can reach 1.5 to 2 meters in favourable conditions.

quiz.q: What is the optimum soil temperature for sunflower seed germination?
quiz.explanation: Sunflower seeds germinate best when soil temperature is between 20 and 25Â°C.

quiz.q: Which part of the sunflower head produces seeds?
quiz.explanation: The disc florets in the centre of the head are fertile and each can produce one seed.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for local tall sunflower varieties?
quiz.explanation: For tall local varieties, a spacing of 75 cm between rows and 30 cm within rows is recommended.

quiz.q: When should you thin sunflower seedlings?
options: B) When they are 10-15 cm tall
quiz.explanation: Thinning is done when seedlings are 10-15 cm tall to leave one plant per station.

quiz.q: What is the role of cotyledons in sunflower seedlings?
options: B) They provide food for the young plant
quiz.explanation: Cotyledons are seed leaves that store food and provide energy until true leaves develop.

quiz.q: Which nutrient deficiency causes purplish stems in sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Phosphorus deficiency often results in purplish discolouration of stems and leaves.

quiz.q: During which growth stage does sunflower need the most water?
quiz.explanation: Water demand is highest during flowering and seed filling; stress then reduces yield.

quiz.q: What is the first sign of flowering in sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Flowering begins when the outer yellow ray petals open.

quiz.q: How can you encourage bee pollination in sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Avoiding pesticides during flowering protects bees and other pollinators.

quiz.q: What is the typical duration from flowering to physiological maturity?
quiz.explanation: Seed development from flowering to maturity takes about 30 to 45 days.

quiz.q: At which stage are sunflower seeds hard and black or striped?
quiz.explanation: At physiological maturity, seeds are hard and have reached their final colour.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for storing sunflower seeds for oil extraction?
quiz.explanation: For safe storage and oil extraction, seed moisture should be below 10%.

quiz.q: Which pest bores into sunflower heads and eats seeds?
quiz.explanation: Helicoverpa (head caterpillar) larvae bore into the head and feed on developing seeds.

quiz.q: What does the R5 stage represent in sunflower growth?
quiz.explanation: R5 is the flowering stage, when disc florets are open and pollination occurs.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid applying nitrogen after R5?
options: B) It delays maturity and reduces oil
quiz.explanation: Late nitrogen promotes vegetative growth, delaying maturity and lowering oil content.

quiz.q: What is the first true leaf stage called?
quiz.explanation: V1 is when the first true leaf appears, about 10-14 days after planting.

quiz.q: How can you test sunflower seed germination before planting?
options: B) Place in moist cloth for 7 days
quiz.explanation: A simple germination test involves keeping 100 seeds in a moist cloth for 7 days and counting sprouts.

quiz.q: What is the recommended plant population per hectare for sunflower?
quiz.explanation: A population of 40,000 to 60,000 plants per hectare is typical for sunflower.

quiz.q: Which disease shows white mould on the back of the sunflower head?
quiz.explanation: Sclerotinia head rot causes white cottony mould on the back of the head.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of applying borax to sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Boron deficiency can cause empty seeds; borax supplies boron.

quiz.q: When should you stop irrigating sunflower?
options: B) When back of head turns brown
quiz.explanation: Stop irrigation when the back of the head turns brown to avoid head rot and lodging.

quiz.q: What is heliotropism in sunflower?
quiz.explanation: Heliotropism is the young sunflower head tracking the sun's movement across the sky.

quiz.q: Which stage is critical for determining seed number?
quiz.explanation: The R1 stage (bud visible) is when water stress can most reduce the number of seeds.

quiz.q: What tool is useful for identifying growth stages in the field?
quiz.explanation: A measuring tape and notebook help you record plant height and stage accurately.

quiz.q: What is the average yield of local sunflower varieties per hectare?
quiz.explanation: Local varieties typically yield 1.5 to 2.5 tonnes per hectare under good management.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid overhead irrigation in the evening?
quiz.explanation: Wet foliage overnight encourages fungal diseases like downy mildew.

quiz.q: At which growth stage does the sunflower plant shift from vegetative to reproductive?
quiz.explanation: R1 marks the visible bud stage, the beginning of the reproductive phase.

quiz.q: What is the main consequence of harvesting sunflower too late?
quiz.explanation: Over-mature heads shatter, causing seed loss before harvest.

quiz.q: How can you protect sunflower from bird damage?
options: B) Use scarecrows or reflective tape
quiz.explanation: Scarecrows, reflective tape, and other bird scarers help reduce bird damage.
